Taliban are waging a war on women in Afghanistan: Zahra Nader
item.description:
Zahra Nader is an Afghan journalist who once worked for The New York Times in Afghanistan. Now living in exile in Canada, she runs Zan Times, an online news portal (zan means "woman" in Dari, one of Afghanistan’s official languages). In an interview with Monzurul Islam for Prothom Alo, Nader spoke about what drew her to journalism, what life is like for Afghan women under Taliban rule, and where she still finds hope. The interview was taken on the sidelines of an event marking the 30th anniversary of the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung (KAS) Media Programme Asia in Chiang Mai, Thailand.

Before we talk about Afghanistan today, could you tell me a little about your childhood? What do you remember about going to school for the first time after your family returned from Iran?

Zahra Nader: My family fled to Iran when the Taliban first took over Afghanistan. I was six. There was a lot of racism against Afghan refugees in Iran. What hurt me most was that I wasn’t allowed to go to school. That left deep scars. Even after all these years, I haven’t forgotten what I went through.

For a long time, my biggest dream was simply to go to school. That’s why what’s happening in Afghanistan today is so personal to me. I know what it means to be denied the right to an education.

My family returned to Afghanistan around 2003, I think, and settled in Kabul. That was when I went to school for the first time. It was about an hour from home and didn’t have a proper building. Most of the classrooms were in tents donated by UNICEF. But I was happy. I could finally go to school, dream of becoming somebody and hope that one day I might serve my country.

What drew you to journalism? Was there a story you covered in Afghanistan that made you feel this was the work you wanted to do?

Zahra Nader: As a child, I wanted to be a teacher. Journalism wasn’t on my list. I came to it by accident. One day I walked into the office of a news weekly in Kabul. I was writing poetry at the time. They published one of my poems and offered me an internship, which I gladly accepted.

I stayed because, as a woman from a marginalised community in Afghanistan, I found some power in journalism. People like me weren’t usually in a position to ask questions, talk about politics or hold people in power to account. Journalism gave me that opportunity.

I remember writing for my university newspaper about the lack of electricity in my neighbourhood. The minister had promised that all of Kabul would have electricity within 40 days. Years later, my neighbourhood still had none. So I asked: Why don’t we have electricity? Why hasn’t it reached our community?

That story helped me see what I could do as a journalist. I could bring problems that were often invisible to the wider public into the conversation. And once people were talking about them, there was at least a chance that something might change.

All our journalists inside Afghanistan use pen names. None of them publishes under her real name. It’s too dangerous. We also withhold our sources’ real names and try to leave out details that could identify either a source or a reporter.

What led you to leave Afghanistan for Canada, and how did the move change your work as a journalist?

Zahra Nader: I was working for The New York Times when I left Afghanistan in 2017. By then, the security situation was very tense. Almost every day on my way to work, I thought a bomb might go off and we could become collateral damage in the war. My son was four. I wanted him to grow up with the rights and opportunities I hadn’t had as a refugee child in Iran.

In Canada, I found it very difficult, if not impossible, to continue working as a journalist. As an Afghan woman who had come to Canada, I didn’t feel encouraged to pursue journalism. Some people suggested I get a job at a coffee shop and have a second child. That was the future they saw for me. It wasn’t the one I wanted.

I went to university instead. I did a master’s in communication and culture and started a PhD in women’s and gender studies. I was doing my PhD in Canada when the Taliban returned to power.

During a discussion at the event, you drew a parallel between the US-led "war on terror" and what the Taliban are doing in Afghanistan. How would you describe what the Taliban are doing to Afghan women, and why do you use those words?

Zahra Nader: When the Taliban took over, women were their first target. In the first week, women were told to stay home and not come to work. Within the first month, girls were told they couldn’t go to school. Then women were shut out of universities. They lost the right to travel on their own and to choose what to wear. The Taliban are waging a war on women in Afghanistan.

I call it a war because the aim is to remove women from society altogether. They are trying to build a dystopia in which only one gender exists in public life: men. That doesn’t mean life is good for men in Afghanistan. But if you look at what the Taliban have done over the past five years, you can see how central the removal of women from public life is to what they’re trying to achieve.

Women did take to the streets at first. The Taliban suppressed the protests and imprisoned women. Some women were killed because of their activism. It’s much harder for women to protest openly now. But I see resistance happening quietly. A woman turns her basement, living room or kitchen into a classroom for six or seven girls from her neighbourhood. I see that as preparation for a life beyond the Taliban.

Can women still work as journalists inside Afghanistan? If a young woman wants to report a story today, what barriers would she face?

Zahra Nader: There’s no decree that explicitly says women are banned from journalism. But the Taliban’s vice and virtue law completely bans women’s voices from being heard and their faces from being seen in public. Women are also required to be accompanied by a male guardian when they go out. All of that affects their ability to report.

In cities like Kabul, there are still some outlets where you might hear a woman narrating a report without showing her face. Some women also work at radio stations in the provinces, sometimes in offices where men and women are kept apart. But they have very little room to report independently, especially on issues such as women’s rights, school closures or women’s health.

Some women work without pay in the hope of getting a letter that says they’ve worked at a station. Their families have to cover the cost of getting them to and from work. They can also be turned away from press conferences. When my colleagues or I call Taliban officials for comment, some refuse to speak to us because they consider it sinful to speak to women. Others simply won’t talk to journalists.

In most parts of Afghanistan, women no longer work openly in the media. But some are still reporting in secret, including for newsrooms in exile like ours.

What made you start Zan Times? What did you want the newsroom to do?

Zahra Nader: I started Zan Times in 2022. I felt a huge sense of responsibility. I also felt guilty. I was safe in Canada, where my rights and freedoms were protected, while millions of Afghan women and girls were losing theirs.

I grew up in Kabul. I went to school and university there. The freedoms I had, however limited, allowed me to get an education, work in public and become a journalist. Now those same opportunities were being denied to millions of women and girls. I felt I had to do something. And I remembered that I was a journalist.

I took leave from my PhD and used my savings to build the newsroom. I thought: If the Taliban are shutting women inside their own homes, can we give them a chance to work from home? Can we train them to become journalists and give them a place to publish their reporting?

That’s why Zan Times exists. We wanted to create opportunities for women journalists and resist the Taliban’s attempt to erase women from Afghan public life.

I hope people in Bangladesh will stand in solidarity with Afghan women. If you feel there’s nothing you can do for Afghanistan, at least learn from what happened to us. Take it as a warning so that it doesn’t happen in your country. And if you can act, one way to show solidarity is to ask your government not to legitimise the Taliban or treat relations with them as normal.

You mentioned that Zan Times received hundreds of applications for just 12 fellowship places. How did that fellowship come about, and what did the response mean to you?

Zahra Nader: In 2024 and 2025, we trained about 70 women from across Afghanistan. We could cover their internet costs, but we couldn’t pay them a stipend. We realised that wasn’t sustainable. How can I expect someone to learn on an empty stomach when she’s thinking about where her next meal will come from?

So we set up a 10-month fellowship for 12 women. We wanted to offer online training and mentoring, as well as a monthly stipend so they could support themselves and their families while learning and working with us.

Applications opened on 19 January 2026 and closed on 5 February. We received 860 applications for 12 places. We were overwhelmed. What inspired us was how many women were still willing to take the risk of becoming journalists and reporting on what was happening in their communities. They still had hope. They wanted to do something.

Your reporters inside Afghanistan use pen names. How do you decide whether a story can be published safely?

Zahra Nader: All our journalists inside Afghanistan use pen names. None of them publishes under her real name. It’s too dangerous. We also withhold our sources’ real names and try to leave out details that could identify either a source or a reporter.

But sometimes leaving out names isn’t enough. If we think publishing a story could put a colleague or a source at risk, we often decide not to run it.

When you hear from young Afghan women who still want to study, work or tell their own stories, what do they say about the future they want? What gives you hope?

Zahra Nader: A colleague in Afghanistan once sent me an interview with a girl who was about 15 or 16. I cried listening to it. There was so much pain in her voice. Even now, when I think of her, I feel sad.

She said the world was moving forward, developing new technology and going to the moon, while Afghan girls couldn’t even walk down the street on their own. They were denied that freedom simply because they were girls. She couldn’t go to school and was weaving carpets. Without an education, she said, she couldn’t see a future for herself. But she wanted people to listen to Afghan girls and make sure this wouldn’t be their future.

Women did take to the streets at first. The Taliban suppressed the protests and imprisoned women. Some women were killed because of their activism. It’s much harder for women to protest openly now. But I see resistance happening quietly. A woman turns her basement, living room or kitchen into a classroom for six or seven girls from her neighbourhood. I see that as preparation for a life beyond the Taliban.

I see hope in the journalists who work with me, too. They know their lives could be at risk if they’re caught reporting for Zan Times. They still choose to do it.

I hope people in Bangladesh will stand in solidarity with Afghan women. If you feel there’s nothing you can do for Afghanistan, at least learn from what happened to us. Take it as a warning so that it doesn’t happen in your country. And if you can act, one way to show solidarity is to ask your government not to legitimise the Taliban or treat relations with them as normal.

item.title: World leaders take stage at COP31 but big names missing
item.description:
TURKEY-UN-POLITICS-DIPLOMACY

World leaders will take the stage at COP31 in Turkey on Wednesday but some prominent names are missing from this year’s annual UN climate summit even as global warming intensifies.

The two-week conference kicked off earlier this week in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with governments under pressure to tackle the climate crisis after a year of heatwaves in Europe, deadly floods in Nepal and major wildfires in Indonesia.

Dozens of leaders will speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian.

But observers have pointed to the absence of some big names, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit.

While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is coming to Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the event.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the most recent list.

“It is a shame that some of the bigger European leaders aren’t coming. We need Europe to be showing up strongly at this COP,” Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think-tank E3G, told AFP.

Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s top climate official, said the absences were “not completely atypical” as leaders may have “practical” reasons for not being able to attend a summit.

But he also told reporters in Brussels that “expectations are not necessarily high” for this climate conference.

Iran’s Pezeshkian said he would use the event as an opportunity to express Tehran’s position on environmental destruction in war.

“At this conference, we will speak about the actions of the United States and Israel in destroying the environment,” he said before departing for Turkey, according to Iranian state television.

The French government said Macron would be absent because November 11 is World War I Armistice Day and the president will attend an EU summit in Ireland on Thursday.

“If top leaders want influence over where the global (energy) transition is going, showing up is a pretty good place to start,” said Chiara Martinelli, director of Climate Action Network Europe.

“I am afraid that Ursula von der Leyen will be lonely on the stage while the leaders of the biggest EU economies are a no-show,” Martinelli said.

‘We have Lula’

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump, who pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and has not sent officials to climate talks since his re-election in 2024, is not attending the summit.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who rarely attends COPs, will be represented by Vice President Han Zheng.

The United States and China are the world’s top economies and biggest emitters of planet-heating emissions, making their presence at climate talks crucial to the process.

“But we have Lula,” Cassel said.

Climate campaigners breathed a huge sigh of relief when Lula, who has championed cutting deforestation rates, defeated right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro in last month’s Brazilian presidential election.

COP31 host Turkey is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with a target of raising electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.

The EU has stressed that electrification must be “clean”, which could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.

Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels -- the main driver of climate change -- nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual COP conferences.

item.title: AJR Courier attacked 15 times in 23 days: who is really behind it?
item.description:
AJR Courier Service has been targeted ever since receiving public threats and facing attacks accompanied by the statement, “We are Captain Imon's men; you will pay us the rent for this place, we will collect it.”

The business entity has come under successive attacks. Over the past 23 days, its warehouses, branch offices, and cargo vehicles have been attacked at least 15 times across various locations in Narayanganj and the capital. At least six employees have been injured, with one suffering burns to nearly 50 per cent of his body. The company has filed three General Diaries (GDs) and five lawsuits over these incidents.

An analysis of the case statement and talks with AJR officials, the trouble began on 18 October. At around 10:30 pm that night, two unidentified men on a motorcycle arrived outside their Hazaribagh office, rented from the Bay Group. One of them threatened the staff, stating that the office would be taken over.

The first physical attack took place on 20 October. In the evening, 70 to 80 armed people, arriving on 35 to 40 motorcycles, attacked their main warehouse near Sikder Medical College in Hazaribagh. Identifying themselves as henchmen of top criminal Imon, they barged inside, vandalised the property, and looted goods.

They made off with items worth approximately Tk 3.1 million, including CCTV cameras, NVRs, and laptops containing critical data. The company's manager, Md Afsar Uddin, filed a case in this connection with Hazaribagh police station on 21 October.

Hazaribagh police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Mosharraf Hossain told Prothom Alo on Sunday that 11 of the accused have been arrested in connection with this case. The names of at least seven more suspects have been obtained, and police are working to apprehend them.

However, Jayanta Chowdhury, assistant general manager (AGM) of the company's Human Resources and Audit Department, maintained that the masterminds behind the attacks remain at large.

He told Prothom Alo, “They are using Captain Imon's name, but we do not know who is actually behind this. Because they haven't been arrested, the attacks on us are not stopping.”

Extortion demands were made by people claiming to represent top criminal Imon. The attacks began soon afterwards, with groups arriving on motorcycles and hurling crude bombs and flammable substances. One employee suffered burn injuries in a petrol bomb attack, while six drivers and staff members were injured.

Addressing this, OC Mosharraf stated that interrogating the 11 arrestees yielded no evidence of anyone named Captain Imon directly operating behind the scene. However, police derived the names of three individuals acting as direct handlers.

They are using encrypted communications technologies, meaning that while their names are known, their exact locations have not yet been traced. They went into hiding immediately after the 20 October incident, but police will track them down regardless of where they are, he added.

Top police-listed criminal Sanjidul Islam Imon is locally known as 'Captain Imon'. According to police intelligence, he is currently hiding abroad.

Relevant sources report that links to top criminal Imon have indeed been traced behind these continuous attacks. Operating from abroad, he controls the underworld in that area.

To target rivals and businesses, he deploys local teen gangs or smaller local groups, engaging different cliques for different assignments and paying them upon completion of specific tasks. Alongside his own network, criminal Imon indirectly commands several local gang units in this manner.

Continuous threats and attacks following police case

On 23 October, at around 11:00 pm—the day after a police case was filed over the initial attack—an unidentified caller phoned the plaintiff, Afsar Uddin. The caller threatened to kill him within 24 hours if he failed to reach a settlement, boasting that he knew his residential address.

At dawn the following day, 24 October, two covered vans parked in front of the Hazaribagh warehouse were vandalised. The company alleged that early on 25 October, petrol was poured near the warehouse’s internet line and behind the toilet facilities to set the premises ablaze. Officials stated that prompt intervention by security guards prevented the fire from escalating.

On the same morning at around 6:30 am, six to seven miscreants intercepted a courier staff member as he was returning home after his shift. After confirming whether he worked for AJR Courier Service, they assaulted him and robbed him of his smartphone and wallet.

Before the dust from these incidents could settle, another attack took place on 26 October near the Shanir Akhra Hanif Flyover roundabout in Jatrabari. Bricks were hurled at a moving covered van, shattering its windscreen.

On 27 October, the target shifted to AJR’s branch office at Arif Market in Fatullah, Narayanganj. At around 2:30 am, petrol or a similar flammable substance was sprayed outside the office and set on fire. Market security guards extinguished the flames.

Following this, two more covered vans were targeted. On the night of 31 October, in the same area of Jatrabari, the windscreens of the two vans were smashed, and one driver was given death threats.

Despite all this, the unidentified perpetrators did not stop. At around midnight on 1 November, an AJR covered van was attacked near the Matsya Bhaban area in Shahbagh. The assailants shattered the vehicle’s glass using iron hammers and hockey sticks. Bricks were thrown at the driver, Ahsan Habib, striking him in the head. He was rushed to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.

Sub-Inspector (SI) Khalek, the investigating officer for the case filed with Shahbagh Police Station, told Prothom Alo that no suspects have been identified so far. The investigation is progressing through footage analysis and evidence collection. However, it is suspected that the attackers acted out of a grudge against AJR.

That very night, another covered van was attacked in the Rayerbazar area of Mohammadpur. The driver was beaten with a steel pipe, pulled out of the vehicle, and robbed of his mobile phone and wallet.

The attackers then hurled a crude bomb (cocktail) into the cabin, setting the vehicle on fire. A case has been registered with Mohammadpur Police Station regarding this incident; however, police have yet to report any progress in identifying the perpetrators.

Staff burnt by petrol bomb; goods worth Tk 10m destroyed

At around 9:15 pm on 3 November, a group of unidentified individuals was loitering outside the company’s office in the Mirpur 11 area of the capital. At one point, they hurled two petrol bombs directly at AJR staff member Md Babul Miah. Catching fire, his body suffered nearly 50 per cent burns. A case was subsequently filed with Pallabi Police Station.

Two days later, at around 9:30 pm on 5 November, an AJR delivery vehicle was attacked in the Rayerbazar area of Mohammadpur. At least 25 to 26 men arriving on 13 motorcycles smashed the vehicle’s glass. When the driver stepped out, they struck his legs with iron rods before tossing crude bombs (cocktails) and petrol bombs into the cabin, setting it ablaze.

Hafizur Rahman Pulak, president, Courier Services Association of BangladeshIt is vital to take necessary steps to stop the attacks and prevent their recurrence. Building up a courier service provider requires immense effort, involving regular tax payments, marketing, and compensating for lost or damaged goods. Incidents such as serial attacks and threats against AJR Courier Service are harmful to any courier firm.

The fire destroyed various goods inside the vehicle, including bank ATM cards, chequebooks, pharmaceuticals, apparel, cosmetics, and auto spare parts. The company claimed damages of approximately Tk 10 million (1 crore). A case regarding this incident was also registered at Mohammadpur Police Station.

Mohammadpur Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Abdul Halim told Prothom Alo that technology-based tracking had yielded no leads to identify the perpetrators following the two incidents. Police are now pursuing local informants.

He added that although the attack occurred in Mohammadpur, it stems primarily from the dispute originating in Hazaribagh; hence, they are coordinating closely with Hazaribagh Police Station.

At around 3:00 am on the night of 4 November, another delivery vehicle was intercepted in the Gulistan Zero Point area under Paltan Police Station. The driver was pulled from the vehicle, choked, and beaten with sticks and iron rods.

Separately, on 4 November, allegations surfaced that a man named Zahir went to the staff quarters in Hazaribagh, threatening employees and attempting to break the locks.

At around 9:30 pm on 7 November, another product-carrying vehicle belonging to the firm was reportedly attacked in the Dhanmondi area.

Company official Jayanta Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that the vehicle was en route to the Hazaribagh warehouse via Mirpur Road. As it reached Road No. 3 in Dhanmondi, miscreants began vandalising the vehicle, dragged driver Mizanur Rahman out, and severely injured him with iron rods. A case is being prepared over the matter.

Later that night, Dhanmondi Police Station OC Muhammad Imdadul Islam Taieb told Prothom Alo, “Neither the victim nor the institution has submitted a formal complaint yet. We are investigating whether this incident stems from the dispute with AJR or a personal grievance involving the driver. However, CCTV footage of the exact spot has not been recovered yet, as cameras on adjacent shopping complexes failed to capture the scene.”

Early on Tuesday morning, AJR Group official Jayanta Chowdhury informed Prothom Alo that several miscreants attacked one of their vehicles on Northbrook Hall Road in Banglabazar at around 9:30 pm on Monday. The attackers threw four petrol bombs in an attempt to torch the vehicle and kill the driver.

The vehicle's windscreen was damaged, but the driver managed to speed away from the scene. At around 10:30 pm on Monday, another transport vehicle was targeted. Two helmet-clad terrorists on a high-speed motorcycle attacked the vehicle, throwing bricks to shatter its glass, he added.

What do police officials think about crude bomb explosions, bus arson attacks?

Nearly 5,000 workers living in insecurity

Mizanur, a driver for the firm directly engaged in nationwide goods transport services, was attacked in the Dhanmondi area on the night of 7 November while heading towards the Hazaribagh warehouse.

Mizanur told Prothom Alo, “Before I could even realise what was happening, miscreants suddenly reached inside through the window in less than a minute, assaulted me, and vandalised the vehicle.” The AJR driver added, “With continuous attacks on our vehicles like this, we cannot transport goods normally. You cannot drive a vehicle while living in terror.”

AJR management claims that at least 5,000 workers are employed at the company, a major portion of whom belong to low-income brackets. Relentless attacks and threats have created panic among employees, leaving goods transport and delivery operations severely compromised.

Jayanta Chowdhury, assistant general manager (AGM) of the company's Human Resources and Audit Department, said, “We have filed police cases and General Diaries (GDs) for eight of the incidents, and complaints will be submitted for the remaining cases as well. However, despite so many complaints, the police are failing to arrest those involved or investigate the matter properly. In the face of such inaction, the attackers are gaining even more courage.”

Hafizur Rahman Pulak, president of the Courier Services Association of Bangladesh, believes it is vital to take necessary steps to stop the attacks and prevent their recurrence. Speaking to Prothom Alo on Monday, he said that building up a courier service provider requires immense effort, involving regular tax payments, marketing, and compensating for lost or damaged goods. Incidents such as serial attacks and threats against AJR Courier Service are harmful to any courier firm.

item.title: Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair
item.description:
USA-STOCKS/NVIDIA

Nvidia shed about $430 billion in market value over two sessions as new reports deepened questions about CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

The controversy escalated on several fronts on Tuesday as allegations emerged that Huang's relationship with Alice Huang aided at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China and that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously briefed President Donald Trump on the affair.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer demanded answers from the administration and tighter curbs on chip exports to China, while the company's independent directors hired outside counsel to investigate.

Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO.

"The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he's got to go," Cramer told Politico late on Tuesday.

The allegations have turned Huang's personal conduct into a broader risk for Nvidia, raising questions about the company's governance and its dependence on the CEO who has led it for more than three decades and built it into the dominant supplier of AI chips.

He owns about 3.6 per cent of the company but does not have majority voting control and runs an unusually flat organization in which dozens of executives report directly to him.

The FBI is separately examining whether 63-year-old Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang has told employees he was unfaithful to his wife, but provided no details about the relationship. China's foreign ministry has said the spy accusations are "groundless."

Huang apologized to top executives at a closed-door meeting on Monday before pivoting to business and was back holding meetings at Nvidia's headquarters on Tuesday, CNBC reported.

Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised and that Huang has committed to cooperating with the internal review. The board has retained Joon Kim, a Wachtell Lipton partner and former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, whose practice includes internal investigations and white-collar defense, to lead the probe.

Nvidia's stock, which had been nearly flat this year before news of the affair broke, has fallen 9.5 per cent since then. The shares have lagged the broader market .SPX on investor unease over whether massive spending on AI will deliver adequate returns.

When did Trump know

The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Rubio had briefed Trump aboard Air Force One en route to China in May about US intelligence indicating Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

The briefing marked at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been told about the intelligence, the Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

Trump said on Monday he had spoken with Huang and asked whether he knew the woman was a spy. Trump said Huang told him he had "absolutely no idea" and that he believed the Nvidia CEO.

Trump also said he had not known about the alleged ties when Huang accompanied him to China in May.

A White House official disputed the report and referred Reuters to Trump's comments on Monday.

Schumer said on Tuesday that Congress must have a full accounting of Trump's defense of Huang and called on lawmakers to quickly approve new restrictions on US chip exports to China.

"He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends," Schumer said, accusing Trump of failing to address foreign espionage in the American technology industry.

US news publication Axios, citing sources, reported on Tuesday that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about the Nvidia CEO's relationship with Alice Huang.

Reuters could not immediately verify that report. The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside regular business hours.

Who is Alice Huang

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, along with her husband and sister, built a network of companies across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, The Information reported.

When orders for Nvidia chips subject to US export restrictions stalled, Alice Huang used ties to Nvidia to secure supplies, helping move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China, according to the report. Some of the chips ultimately served Alibaba 9988.HK, Tencent 0700.HK and smaller Chinese AI labs.

Reuters could not determine Alice Huang's whereabouts to seek comment.

She held senior roles ​at a Shanghai investment firm before becoming the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International, which was linked to Century Litong, a China-based company that secured preferred cloud partner status with Nvidia in 2023, giving it priority access to the company's chips.

Separately, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday that several US government agencies pushed for Megaspeed to be included on the entity list, a trade blacklist of groups connected to China that US officials say pose national security risks, but the US Commerce Department was delaying efforts to blacklist the company.

The Commerce Department had sought more information about some companies under consideration, the FT reported. It was unclear whether Megaspeed was among those companies, but the delay has left it off the list, according to the report.

The US Department of Commerce and Nvidia did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Alibaba, Tencent, Megaspeed and Century Litong were not immediately available for comment outside regular business hours. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.

item.title: Tarique Rahman-Erdogan meet takes Bangladesh-Turkiye ties to new strategic height: Humaiun
item.description:
Bangladesh-Turkiye relations have reached a new strategic height through the bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said here.

The meeting, held at the Max Royal Hotel in Antalya on Tuesday evening, discussed expanding cooperation in various sectors, including trade and investment, energy, aviation and the defence industry.

Both sides expressed interest in exploring the possibility of building a defence industry in Bangladesh and of joint investment in the sector, said the state minister at a press conference on Tuesday night at the Papillon Ziugma Relaxury Hotel in Antalya.

Humaiun Kobir said the meeting between the Bangladesh Prime Minister and the Turkish President took place in a warm and fraternal atmosphere. President Erdogan addressed Prime Minister Tarique Rahman as “my valuable friend and brother” and expressed interest in taking relations with Bangladesh to a higher level.

Along with increasing bilateral trade and investment, partnership in the energy sector, investment in aviation and cooperation in the defence industry received importance at the meeting.

Humaiun Kobir said the Bangladesh government has taken an initiative to set up a defence industrial park in the country. Prospects of Turkish investment and joint ventures in this sector were discussed. However, he said, no agreement or memorandum of understanding (MoU) has yet been signed on the matter, which remains at the stage of preliminary exploration and discussion.

He said discussions on energy covered deep-sea mineral and energy exploration, renewable energy and making use of Turkiye’s experience and best practices in these areas.

Bangladesh is keen to build a strong investment partnership with Turkiye in these sectors.

Speaking on the Rohingya crisis, the state minister said the two leaders discussed the safe, peaceful and sustainable repatriation of the Rohingyas. They also exchanged views on how to advance joint efforts further after the hearing on the Rohingya issue at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) this month.

He said Bangladesh and Turkiye discussed working together to ensure the safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingyas to their homeland. The meeting also touched on strengthening mutual cooperation on important issues concerning the Muslim world.

The state minister said Bangladesh wants to play a leading role among the countries of the Global South in tackling climate change and in climate finance. Bangladesh is not only a victim of climate change, he said, but is also playing an active role in raising international awareness and demanding easier access to climate finance.

He said Bangladeshi representatives would take part in various thematic dialogues and sessions of COP31 and present Bangladesh’s position on climate adaptation, finance and loss and damage.

Humaiun Kobir said President Erdogan is holding bilateral meetings with only a few of the leaders attending COP31 and that the meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman reflects Turkiye’s special interest in and importance attached to Bangladesh.

He said Bangladesh is moving forward in the international arena with new prospects under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. Following the democratic transition, international interest in the new government of Bangladesh is also growing.

The state minister said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman invited President Erdogan and his wife to visit Bangladesh.

He said the Prime Minister has several important engagements today (Wednesday) including bilateral meetings with heads of state and government of various countries and a meeting with the UK foreign secretary.

State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Environment, Forest and Climate Change Md Saimum Parvez, Press Secretary AAM Saleh Shibli and Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu were present at the press conference.

item.title: Now BUET rejects UGC recommendation, admission test to go ahead as scheduled
item.description:
Following Dhaka University (DU), the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) has also confirmed that its admission test for the 2026–27 academic year will be held according to the previously announced schedule.

In a notice issued on Tuesday (10 November), BUET said it had decided not to change the examination date. The first-year undergraduate admission test will be held on 16 January next year.

Earlier, the University Grants Commission (UGC) held a meeting with the vice-chancellors of public universities on Monday. At the meeting, it was decided that admission tests for the 2026–27 academic year would be held after 1 February next year.

Discussions were also held on starting the application process after 1 January. 

Following the UGC meeting, Dhaka University announced that it would stick to its original examination schedule. BUET has now also decided to follow its previously announced date.

There was no preliminary screening test for admission to BUET in the 2025–26 academic year. Instead, candidates eligible for admission were selected solely through a written examination. 

BUET's latest notice did not specify whether the same procedure would be followed this year. The university said the application deadline and other details would be announced in a subsequent notice.

Meanwhile, supplementary examinations for students who failed in one or two subjects in the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will begin on 1 December 2026. 

Even if any of the approximately 420,000 students who failed in one or two subjects pass the supplementary examinations, they will effectively be ineligible to sit the admission tests at BUET and the Dhaka University.

item.title: “Will I have to live without my mother?”: 4-year-old Maimuna asks her father
item.description:
Six days after giving birth to her third child, Meherun Nesa, 25, was busy hosting the guests at a grand aqiqah ceremony organised to celebrate the newborn. She later had a fever the following day. Her physical condition deteriorated rapidly thereafter. Just 13 days after giving birth, Meherun Nesa passed away.

Meherun was the wife of Monirul Islam from Member Bari in the Masterhat area of Shikolbaha Union in Karnaphuli Upazila, Chattogram. She died of dengue last Friday (6 November). The couple have three daughters. Their two older daughters are seven and just over four years old.

Ever since their mother’s death, the two older daughters have spent their days in tears. While the eldest daughter Miftahul Jannat weeps silently, the second daughter Maimuna Jannat frequently breaks down into loud sobs. Over and over, she asks her father, "Will I have to live without my mother?"

Monirul Islam has no answer to his daughter's question. He is also devastated by his wife's death. Whenever Meherun's name comes up, he silently wipes away his tears.

During a visit to their home at around 4:30 pm on Monday, Monirul was seen sitting inside the house while his two daughters, Miftahul and Maimuna, were in the courtyard. Relatives were coming and going, stopping along the way to gently pat the girls on the head.

Monirul said his youngest daughter Nusaiba Jannat was born on 25 October. The family arranged her aqiqah ceremony six days later. Meherun developed a fever the following day. She initially bought medicine from a pharmacy but there was no improvement. Her temperature eventually reached 105 degrees Fahrenheit. A physician then advised a dengue test.

The test confirmed that Meherun had dengue. She was taken to a private hospital in the city, where physicians admitted her to the intensive care unit (ICU).

As her condition worsened, she was transferred to another private hospital on Thursday afternoon. She was placed on life support that night. The attending physician declared her dead the following day, on Friday.

Monirul said he married Meherun in 2019. Fighting back tears, he said, “It is extremely difficult for me to accept my wife's death. My youngest daughter, Nusaiba, has not even had the chance to know what a mother's affection feels like. How will I manage with three little children? Who will take care of my youngest?”

Monirul said his seven-year-old daughter had become unusually quiet since her mother's death, while the four-year-old constantly looked for her mother.

Meherun's father, Abu Taher, was also at Monirul's house. “I can hardly console Monirul. My heart aches for my three granddaughters,” he said.
