item.title: The land we share: Bangladesh’s stories of harmony
item.description:
In a village in Indian Punjab, 87-year-old Gajju Khan is waiting for a sound he has not heard for most of his life. He wants to live long enough to hear the call to prayer from the mosque now being built in Jakhiwal.
What makes the story more striking is who is building it. Local Sikhs and Hindus have given money, bricks, cement, and land so that their Muslim neighbours can finally have a place to pray.
Independent journalist Cheena Kapoor wrote about this in a photo essay published on October 28, 2026 . It shows villagers restoring mosques that were abandoned after the violence and mass displacement of the 1947 Partition.
One of them is Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh woman who persuaded her grandson to donate the family’s farmland for the mosque. Her reasoning was simple. The other community has a place to gather. The local Muslims do not.
The Partition tore countless families apart, and the wound has been carried from one generation to the next. That is why the weight of this effort is so great. There are no grand declarations about tolerance here. It began with a piece of land, an unmet need, and a few neighbours willing to stand by.
As the mosque rises, something invisible is being joined to it: The everyday trust of living side by side.
Bangladesh has its own stories too, and they are not cast in one mould. In some places there are mutual gifts of land, in others a closed place of worship has been allowed to reopen, and in others neighbours have quietly made sure no one in the community went without what they needed.
A mosque and a crematorium in Bagerhat
In Fakirhat, Bagerhat, two people of different faiths each met a need of the other’s community. According to a report published in April 2022 , Pranab Kumar Ghosh, a Hindu college teacher, donated land for a mosque, while Sheikh Mizanur Rahman, a local Muslim politician, gave land for a Hindu crematorium.
After the Dhaka-Khulna highway opened, Attaki Mor (crossing) became much busier. Shopkeepers and passers-by there struggled to find a place to pray. On the land Ghosh gave, a small prayer room was built first, and a larger mosque grew up around it later.
The crematorium problem was of a different kind. The old one on the bank of the Bhairab river had been swallowed by the river, leaving Hindu families with nowhere to perform last rites. Mizanur Rahman, who owned the adjoining land, gave a portion of it for a new crematorium.
The needs were different, but the understanding was the same: You respect your neighbour’s religious obligations even when they are not your own.
Ghosh’s college later recognized his contribution, and local leaders held up both initiatives as examples of harmony. Most striking of all, the generosity went both ways, and neither man was asked to embrace the other’s faith.
A temple reopens after 47 years in Rajshahi
In Rajshahi, generosity took the form of an unlocked door. Regular puja had not been held at the Khojapur Sarbojanin Shib and Kali Matar Mondir (temple) since 1975. The land the temple stands on had been bought by Korban Ali, a Muslim businessman.
When local devotees wanted to reopen the temple, he agreed. In March 2022, devotees returned to observe Maha Shivratri, and to make the way easier, Ali even removed two mango trees himself.
A report captures the emotion and weight of that first major puja in 47 years. The path to the temple had become hard to reach, and Ali let the devotees walk through his own land.
No land changed hands here, yet the episode matters just as much. Ownership of land could easily have meant a locked gate. Ali instead made room for his Hindu neighbours.
A reopened temple cannot erase decades of silence, but it has given one community back a place tied to its faith and history.
When the state makes room
Government institutions have given land too. In October 2018, the then prime minister announced a gift of about one and a half bigha of adjoining land to the Dhakeshwari Temple, one of the country’s most important Hindu places of worship.
In August 2025, Bangladesh Railway allotted land in Dhaka’s Joar Sahara area for two mosques and a Hindu temple at a nominal price set by the railway authority.
These were not acts of personal kindness, and it would be wrong to read them that way. One was the announcement of a political leader holding public office, the other an institutional allocation.
Their value lies in a public message: Different communities in the same city need safe places to worship. But how much of that value becomes real depends on what happens after the announcement: The legal transfer, how the land is used, and whether the institution can actually put it to use.
Where land is held by a public agency, transparent rules and fair access matter most.
Interfaith help is not always about land. A two-day Harinam Moha yogga of Matua devotees, held in April 2026, took place at Bangladesh Ashwini Sebashram in Ganga Channa village, Chitalmari upazila, Bagerhat. There were rituals, devotional songs, and a local fair. People of other faiths, including Muslims, volunteered to provide water, resting arrangements, and other services.
These acts may seem modest, but big gatherings run on help passed from hand to hand. A neighbour who offers water or shelter can be part of the event without taking part in the rituals. The only thing asked in return is that we give a neighbour’s festival the same consideration we hope for our own.
A neighbour’s land, a young man’s future
Generosity can reach beyond places of worship. According to a report published in October 2026, a Hindu resident of Juri in Moulvibazar donated some land to his Muslim neighbour. The young man had got a job at Sonali Bank but ran into trouble during the recruitment verification. His family lived in a rented house, and no immovable property was registered in his father’s name. The land was given free of charge, and the donor also paid the registration costs. A sub-registrar confirmed the transfer, though the report did not name the parties.
This was not a gift for a mosque, temple or church, yet it belongs to the same story: How people respond to one another’s needs across religious lines.
Sometimes the most meaningful help is not a building or a public event. It is an opportunity that might otherwise have been lost.
Religious communities have also stood together by donating land for their own places of worship. In Chittagong, former president Ziaur Rahman gave land for the Purnachar International Buddhist Temple and guest house, as mentioned in a report.
Three acres of land donated by a parish secretary and other members in Tangail helped establish St John’s Church in Sridampara village, where about 65 Garo families worship. Neither account proves donations across faiths, but both show how land and community contributions can sustain religious life.
Harmony does not mean the absence of disagreement
These stories are not all of one kind. Some are personal generosity, some are government decisions, some are practical help, and each has to be understood in its own context. Nor does a handful of good examples mean that religious minorities never face discrimination, insecurity, or property disputes.
Harmony cannot be measured by counting how many temples, mosques, and churches stand side by side. It depends on whether people can worship freely, whether property rights are protected, whether the authorities settle disputes fairly, and whether neighbours can trust one another without fear.
A donation can be generous, but the chance to worship should never depend on one landowner’s goodwill. It is a right, and state institutions must protect it.
The Rajshahi temple stayed shut for 47 years and reopened only because one owner agreed, which is exactly the kind of fragility a right is meant to remove. Empathy strengthens the bonds of coexistence, but it cannot replace equal citizenship, accountability, and the rule of law.
That is why these stories should be told without exaggeration. They do not prove that harmony has been won for good. They only show that people can make it possible in their own neighbourhoods if they choose to.
In Punjab, an old man waits for the call to prayer. In Bagerhat, land gave one community a place to pray and another a place for last rites. In Rajshahi, a temple door opened after decades. In Dhaka, public land has been set aside for different faiths. In Moulvibazar, a neighbour’s small plot secured a young man’s future.
The circumstances differ from place to place. The principle stays the same: Nothing says that another person’s faith, grief, festival, or need has to set us apart.
A piece of land cannot erase the violence of history, and one generous act cannot guarantee a peaceful future. But when people make room for one another, they build something no declaration can: A place where neighbours can pray, mourn, celebrate and belong.
Perhaps that is where harmony begins, with the recognition that everyone has a right to dignity, safety and a place in society, and that protecting it is a public duty, not a private favour.
Nafew Sajed Joy is a Bangladeshi researcher, writer and environmental activist. He has a deep interest in sustainable development, development issues and South Asian affairs.

item.title: General strike over housing hits Spain ahead of election
item.description:
Protesters disrupted the morning commute for hundreds of thousands of Spaniards on Wednesday as a general strike centred on the country’s chronic housing crisis began weeks before a snap election.
Unions reported a “massive” early uptake in Spain’s first nationwide 24-hour stoppage since 2012, which also aims to raise pressure on wages and public services, but business leaders played down the participation.
The size of demonstrations planned in Madrid and Barcelona will be seen as an indicator of public discontent before the November 29 vote, which the right-wing opposition is predicted to win.
The impact on industry and services in the European Union’s fourth-largest economy will also be scrutinized, as pickets were organized at logistics centers, industrial estates and on motorways across the country.
In Madrid, dozens of protesters braved the rain and blocked a main road leading into the center of the Spanish capital, causing tailbacks, but many shops opened as normal.
Public transport suffered disruption even with the implementation of minimum service requirements for commuter trains, metros and buses.
In Barcelona, the metro and bus networks were out of action until the late afternoon after offering minimum services during the morning rush hour.
In contrast, Madrid’s metro reported that 93 percent of its trains ran in the early morning, although passenger numbers were down by around half.
UGT union leader Pepe Alvarez told public broadcaster RTVE that the participation was “massive,” with a “total” stoppage in some regions making the strike “a huge success.”
But UGT spokesman Rafael Espartero acknowledged participation was “uneven,” with large mobilization in the car manufacturing, petrochemicals and meat sectors and in coastal regions, where he said housing difficulties were acute.
The CEOE organization, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.
The main UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner.
The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.
Sanchez, who has governed since 2018 but trails in most polls, has urged voters to defend hard-won rights including public healthcare, the eight-hour working day and pensions amid warnings from his Socialists that the right could roll them back.
But the unions have insisted the strike is directed against all levels of the state and not only the right, which voted down the government’s housing decrees.
The Socialists and the main right-wing opposition Popular Party (PP) “must listen to us, because the streets are speaking clearly”, UGT leader Alvarez said on Wednesday.
Business groups and the right have rejected the strike, seeing an election-related gambit instead of a genuine labor dispute.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who leads most polls, warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike.
Feijoo has also called it a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.
Union leaders have defended the walkout as an exceptional measure intended to generate broad social pressure for action on soaring housing costs.
They are demanding a larger public housing stock, a ban on evicting vulnerable tenants as well as rent controls and restrictions on tourist accommodation in areas suffering the greatest stress.

item.title: US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief
item.description:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party’s crushing midterm election defeat.
The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote Wednesday on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.
The impeachment drive had threatened to deepen Trump’s troubles after Democrats swept last week’s midterms, with anger at the sputtering Iran war and soaring fuel prices helping drive voters to a historic rejection of Republicans.
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And 11 Democrats missed the vote.
Trump hailed the procedural defeat as an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” in a post on Truth Social, while Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, called the vote as a “TOTAL VICTORY!”
“We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest,” Parnell added.
Hegseth earlier Tuesday dismissed the impeachment effort as a “farce” and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations “slander” and “sabotage.”
Moments after Hegseth’s televised appearance, Trump signaled his support.
“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS,” the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Vice President JD Vance also backed the defense secretary, saying he had “obviously not” committed impeachable offenses.
Massie’s eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorization.
Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded “extrajudicial killings.”
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended the operations in Yemen, Iran, Venezuela and against alleged drug smugglers, while seeking to equate the impeachment effort with an attack on US troops.
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said.
The decision to send the resolution to committee halts the immediate impeachment drive but does not prevent Democrats from reviving the effort after taking control of Congress in January.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress at the end of his term.

item.title: World leaders take stage at COP31 but big names missing
item.description:
World leaders will take the stage at COP31 in Turkiye on Wednesday but some prominent names are missing from this year’s annual UN climate summit even as global warming intensifies.
The two-week conference kicked off earlier this week in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with governments under pressure to tackle the climate crisis after a year of heatwaves in Europe, deadly floods in Nepal and major wildfires in Indonesia.
Dozens of leaders will speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian.
But observers have pointed to the absence of some big names, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit.
While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is coming to Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the event.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the most recent list.
“It is a shame that some of the bigger European leaders aren’t coming. We need Europe to be showing up strongly at this COP,” Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think-tank E3G, told AFP.
Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s top climate official, said the absences were “not completely atypical” as leaders may have “practical” reasons for not being able to attend a summit.
But he also told reporters in Brussels that “expectations are not necessarily high” for this climate conference.
Iran’s Pezeshkian said he would use the event as an opportunity to express Tehran’s position on environmental destruction in war.
“At this conference, we will speak about the actions of the United States and Israel in destroying the environment,” he said before departing for Turkiye, according to Iranian state television.
The French government said Macron would be absent because November 11 is World War I Armistice Day and the president will attend an EU summit in Ireland on Thursday.
“If top leaders want influence over where the global (energy) transition is going, showing up is a pretty good place to start,” said Chiara Martinelli, director of Climate Action Network Europe.
“I am afraid that Ursula von der Leyen will be lonely on the stage while the leaders of the biggest EU economies are a no-show,” Martinelli said.
Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump, who pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and has not sent officials to climate talks since his re-election in 2024, is not attending the summit.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who rarely attends COPs, will be represented by Vice President Han Zheng.
The United States and China are the world’s top economies and biggest emitters of planet-heating emissions, making their presence at climate talks crucial to the process.
“But we have Lula,” Cassel said.
Climate campaigners breathed a huge sigh of relief when Lula, who has championed cutting deforestation rates, defeated right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro in last month’s Brazilian presidential election.
COP31 host Turkiye is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with a target of raising electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035.
The EU has stressed that electrification must be “clean,” which could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels -- the main driver of climate change -- nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual COP conferences.

item.title: US judge rejects BBC bid to dismiss Trump defamation suit
item.description:
A federal judge has allowed US President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar defamation suit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting a bid by the British broadcaster to dismiss the case.
Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing a documentary to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
He has sought at least $5 billion each for one claim of defamation and a separate claim under a Florida consumer protection law.
US District Judge Jeffrey T Kuntz on Tuesday rejected the BBC’s bid to dismiss the defamation suit, but tossed the Florida protection law claim.
A spokesperson for the BBC said in a brief statement that the broadcaster was “surprised by this decision” but respected the court’s authority.
“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” the statement added.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, hailed the judge’s ruling as “A Huge Victory.”
“We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” he added.
The BBC documentary at issue spliced together two separate sections of Trump’s speech on January 6, 2021, making it appear that he had explicitly urged supporters to attack the US Capitol.
While the broadcaster has apologized for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, it has denied causing Trump any real injury.
In a 40-page ruling, Kuntz wrote: “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day.”
He added: “Given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement.
“This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”
Last month, Trump faced a setback in the case when a magistrate judge ordered him to give a deposition by December 11, after the BBC claimed he was dodging their efforts to get sworn testimony.
Trump risks sanctions if he fails to attend the deposition by then, including the potential dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.

item.title: Police seal Sylhet resort where fugitive ex-MP Ranjit held meeting
item.description:
Police have sealed Sohel Square Eco Resort in Ratargul, Gowainghat, Sylhet, after fugitive former Sunamganj-1 MP Ranjit Sarkar held a meeting there, triggering widespread controversy.
According to Gowainghat police, the resort was sealed on Wednesday.
Repeated calls to Gowainghat police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Omar Faruk went unanswered. However, duty officer Sub-Inspector Hasib said the Sohel Square Resort in Ratargul was shut down by police around 3am.
Four people, including two resort employees and two Awami League leaders and activists, have been detained in connection with the incident. Police said preparations for filing a case were underway.
According to police and other sources, a lawyer rented the resort on November 8, claiming he would organise an educational tour. More than 150 people arrived at the venue by bus around 3pm and took part in various activities.
Ranjit, joint secretary of Sylhet district Awami League, later appeared at the resort, put up a separate banner, delivered a brief speech and left shortly afterwards.
In a video circulated on social media, he was heard saying that he had held a rally with party leaders and activists after entering the country. He also vowed to continue the struggle until Sheikh Hasina returned to Bangladesh and urged activists to prepare for a final fight.
Ranjit had been in hiding since August 5, 2024, and was reportedly staying in the United Kingdom for a period.
He uploaded the meeting's video to his Facebook account at 4:49pm on Monday. Hours after the footage went viral, an agitated group set fire to his house in Gopaltilla, Sylhet city.
Sunamganj police later arrested Tahirpur upazila Awami League Organising Secretary Tara Mia after identifying him in the video. He was subsequently sent to jail on a court order.
Sources said the meeting was organised under the leadership of local Awami League and Jubo League leaders, including Farid Ahmed Shamim, Aminur Rahman Chowdhury and Masuk Ahmed.
Meanwhile, Ranjit's whereabouts remain unknown. In a WhatsApp conversation with a news outlet, he claimed the meeting was held inside Bangladesh, in his electoral constituency, with only local residents attending.
Acknowledging that the Awami League was banned, he said party leaders would hold programmes wherever they found an opportunity.

item.title: Hasnat questions fertilizer dealership appointments over alleged nepotism
item.description:
Questions over alleged favoritism in the distribution of fertilizer dealerships have emerged after claims that relatives of sitting lawmakers were among those awarded dealerships under a nationwide appointment process.
Hasnat Abdullah, member of parliament for Comilla-4, alleged that the beneficiaries included the wives, sons, nieces and other relatives of sitting MPs, raising concerns over transparency in the selection process.
He said the appointment process was marked by unprecedented corruption and asked the agriculture minister whether it would be reconsidered.
The opposition MP raised the allegations in a supplementary question to the minister during Wednesday afternoon's parliamentary session, presided over by Deputy Speaker Barrister Kaiser Kamal.
Citing several newspaper headlines, Hasnat told the House: “An MP's son, brother-in-law and nephew's wife have become fertilizer dealers. In Thakurgaon, 28 of the 31 dealers are affiliated with the BNP, and 10 of them are wives, children and nieces of party leaders.”
He also noted that a Chhatra Dal leader had been fatally attacked in Natore and that a child of an MP was also alleged to have received a dealership.
Hasnat described the appointments as a “grand festival” of favoritism.
Addressing the minister, he asked whether the irregularities were premeditated, whether the appointments would be reviewed, and when MPs would cease to exploit their positions for the commercial benefit of themselves and their families.
Agriculture Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid responded that 2 committees had been constituted to oversee the appointments: one at the upazila level, chaired by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO), and another at the district level, chaired by the Deputy Commissioner (DC).
He said applications had been invited under specified rules and conditions, and that the ministry had instructed both committees to adhere strictly to those rules.
According to the minister, applications were first forwarded to the upazila level, where the UNO-led committee, together with the upazila agriculture officer, the relevant local agriculture officer and local dignitaries, conducted the initial scrutiny.
The vetted proposals were then submitted to the DC's office, where the district committee reviewed them and sent a ranked list of 3 candidates to the ministry.
The ministry declared the first-ranked candidate the dealer.
The minister added that the district committee comprised the district agriculture officer, the DC and other relevant officials. All proposals reached the ministry bearing the signatures of every committee member rather than that of any single individual.

item.title: Wave of blasts, arson spread fear beyond Dhaka
item.description:
A wave of crude bomb explosions, bus arson and suspected sabotage across Dhaka and several districts has heightened public anxiety, with people increasingly afraid to travel.
The death of a sleeping bus driver in a fire in Faridpur has added to concerns over safety on the roads.
Incidents have been reported in Dhaka, Gazipur, Manikganj, Gopalganj, Faridpur, Chittagong and other districts in recent days, targeting major roads, bus terminals, educational institutions and government establishments.
Police have blamed supporters of a banned political organisation for the incidents, while opposition lawmakers have accused the government of failing to maintain law and order. The government, however, says isolated incidents do not reflect an overall deterioration in the security situation.
On Monday, at least 15 crude bomb explosions and two bus arson attacks were reported in different parts of Dhaka. A bus was set on fire beneath Farmgate Metro Rail Station, while another parked bus was torched in Mirpur-11. Explosions were also reported near Dhaka University, the CMM Court premises, Tejgaon, Uttara, Adabor and Banani.
Outside the capital, two buses were set on fire at separate times in Chandura, Gazipur. Manikganj reported explosions near the deputy commissioner’s office, the police superintendent’s residence and other locations. Similar incidents occurred in Gopalganj, while police reported arrests and the recovery of explosives in several districts.
In Faridpur, bus driver Kalachan Sheikh died after a fire broke out in a parked bus at the new bus terminal early Tuesday. He was sleeping inside and was taken to hospital after becoming ill from smoke inhalation, but doctors declared him dead.
The incidents have alarmed parents, commuters and transport workers. One mother in Mohammadpur said she sent her daughter to school only because she had an examination, adding that she would otherwise have kept her home. Other parents said the frequent explosions and arson attacks had made them afraid to take their children outside.
Business owners and drivers also reported a decline in evening activity. A driver said he continued working despite the risks because he had no alternative, asking where transport workers’ safety could be guaranteed.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police spokesperson Deputy Commissioner Md Akter Hossain said the incidents were being investigated and several people had been arrested. He said at least 33 people were caught in connection with explosions and sabotage attempts in the capital over the previous 24 hours, although the political affiliations of all those detained had not been established.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said police would take legal action against those responsible, describing them as criminals.
In parliament on Tuesday, opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam accused the government of failing to control the deteriorating law and order situation. Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman also questioned the effectiveness of law enforcement agencies.
In response, Salahuddin said authorities were taking action and argued that a handful of incidents did not prove that the country’s overall security situation had become critical. He alleged that ousted forces were attempting to destabilise the country, with possible support from across the border.
University of Dhaka criminologist Dr Touhidul Haque said the perpetrators, their political identities and motives must be established through investigation rather than speculation. He called for stronger law enforcement and intelligence surveillance, while stressing that the government, police, elected representatives and other stakeholders must work together without harassing innocent people.

item.title: Courtroom escapes expose glaring security gaps in Dhaka
item.description:
Two accused in separate murder cases have escaped from Dhaka courtrooms within a month, raising fresh concerns over security arrangements at court premises, including police vigilance, manpower shortages and surveillance gaps.
The latest incident occurred on Tuesday, when Md Kawsar Mia, an accused in the murder of garment worker Alo Akter, removed his handcuffs and fled from the dock of the Dhaka First Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court.
At around 12:40pm, Kawsar was appearing before the court of Acting Judge Mosaddeq Minhaj for a witness hearing. As no witnesses appeared, the court set January 28 for the next hearing. Constable Arafat, responsible for escorting the accused, had placed him in handcuffs in the dock. Kawsar escaped when the constable moved towards the front of the courtroom.
On October 6, another accused, Shariful Islam, escaped while being taken from a courtroom to the court lock-up after appearing before a metropolitan magistrate in a case filed with Kotwali Police Station.
Shariful had also escaped from the Dhaka Third Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court on June 19, 2025, in a murder case involving a teenager in Khilgaon. He allegedly assaulted a police officer and removed his handcuffs while being escorted from the courtroom.
The October case in which he was produced for testimony stemmed from his earlier escape. His second escape has further highlighted weaknesses in the court’s custody arrangements.
Sources at the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) prosecution division said around 500 accused are brought to the Dhaka Judge Court and Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court every day. A total of 438 police personnel are assigned to escort and guard them, but not all are available for the task at all times due to leave and other duties.
Police officials said manpower shortages make it difficult to provide additional security to accused in serious cases. However, they also identified negligence and lack of vigilance among escort personnel as major factors behind the escapes.
DMP Deputy Commissioner (Prosecution) Mohiuddin Mahmud Sohel said cases had been filed over the latest escapes and two police personnel had been temporarily suspended over alleged negligence. Police are also conducting operations to recapture the fugitives.
He said the accused often get an opportunity to escape when escorting constables leave them unattended while collecting custody warrants from court staff. He stressed the need to ensure that handcuffs are properly secured and that officers remain vigilant throughout the process.
Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court Public Prosecutor Omar Faruq Faruqi also blamed negligence and inadequate vigilance. He called for more police personnel and the deployment of experienced officers to escort the accused.
Security concerns extend beyond police escorts. More than half of the CCTV cameras installed at court premises are reportedly out of order, limiting surveillance of courtrooms, corridors, stairways, lock-ups and exits.
There are also complaints about uncontrolled access to court premises, with vendors, suspected pickpockets and other unauthorised people reportedly moving around without proper searches. Although police are stationed at the main gates, visitors are not always checked, according to people familiar with the situation.
Previous incidents underline the recurring nature of the problem. On February 17, 2025, rape case accused Shahidul Islam escaped from the Dhaka Chief Judicial Magistrate Court premises after removing his handcuffs. He was arrested a month later.
On November 16, 2024, robbery case accused Arifur Rahman fled from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court after being ordered to be sent to jail.
In November 2022, two militants were snatched from police custody at a Dhaka court. Reports at the time pointed to failures to follow security procedures, including the use of handcuffs, bulletproof vests and helmets.
Lawyers and officials say preventing further escapes requires more than filing cases and suspending personnel after incidents. They call for clear escort protocols, adequate staffing based on the risk posed by each accused, functional CCTV cameras, proper searches at entry points and accountability for officers on duty.
Repeated escapes from court premises have raised questions not only about police security but also about the safety of the judicial process. According to experts, lasting improvements will require coordinated action rather than temporary measures after each incident.

item.title: Crude bomb explosions at DU: Two pro-AL officials, employees suspended
item.description:
The Dhaka University (DU) administration has temporarily suspended 2 officials and employees over their alleged involvement in crude bomb explosions and attempts to create instability on campus, citing preliminary evidence of their involvement. They have also been issued show-cause notices.
The suspended individuals are Nipu Islam Tonni, a section officer of the Education-1 branch of the university's Registrar's Office, and Mohammad Amanullah, a sanitary supervisor at the Estate Office.
The information was disclosed in a press release issued by the university's Public Relations Office on Wednesday.
Both Tonni and Amanullah were leaders of the currently banned Bangladesh Chhatra League during their student lives.
Tonni was the former president of the Chhatra League's Shamsun Nahar Hall unit at Dhaka University. She was elected as a member in the 2019 Dhaka University Central Students' Union (DUCSU) election.
Amanullah was a former deputy secretary of the central Chhatra League and a former deputy publicity secretary of the organization's Shaheed Sergeant Zahurul Haque Hall unit.
There are also allegations that he took part in a procession of pro-Awami League officials and employees at the Dhaka University Registrar Building on August 4, 2024.
However, Amanullah has denied the allegations against him. He claimed that he performed his official duties on the day of the incident and had no involvement in the explosion.
Several attempts were made to contact Tonni on her mobile phone, but she could not be reached.
The press release said a case had already been filed with Shahbagh police station over the crude bomb explosion on November 10 on the premises of the university's Faculty of Business Studies. The administrative action was taken against the concerned officials and employees after preliminary evidence of their involvement in the incident was found.
The press release further said the university administration remains alert against such acts of sabotage to maintain a peaceful environment, security and stability on campus. Necessary administrative measures are being taken against those involved in such incidents in accordance with the university's existing regulations.
When asked about the matter, Amanullah told Dhaka Tribune: “I have no involvement whatsoever in the crude bomb explosion. I did not participate in any such activities, did not assist anyone, and had no prior knowledge of this matter.”
According to Amanullah, he arrived at the office at 9am on November 10. Later, on the instructions of Estate Manager Fatima Binte Mostafa, he went to different locations of the university with Assistant Estate Manager Abdur Rahim, Chief Assistant Mostafizur Rahman and peon Sujon to collect information related to cleanliness.
During this time, he visited various places, including International Hall, Provost Complex, Faculty of Business Studies, Arts Building, DUCSU, Madhur Canteen, Shahbagh, Doel Chattar, Curzon Hall, Mall Chattar and Muqarram Bhaban. He took photographs of the dirt and garbage at these places and recorded the necessary information. He returned to the office at 1:10pm.
He further said that at 1:20pm, he went to his residence in the South Nilkhet residential area. After receiving a phone call from Security Officer Monir at 2:45pm, he left his residence at 2:50pm and returned to the office.
He then went to the Dhaka Education Board with the officer for official purposes and returned to the office at around 3:45pm. Later, after receiving a phone call from the Estate Manager, he went to the vice-chancellor's office.
After seeing leaders and activists of Shibir protesting there, he left the place and departed from the campus.
He further said: “I demand an impartial investigation based on specific information and evidence.”

item.title: Top Glove recruits 379 workers for Malaysia at zero cost
item.description:
The process of sending workers to Malaysia at zero cost through the state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) has commenced following discussions and scrutiny.
If all goes as scheduled, the selected workers are expected to depart for Malaysia next month.
However, questions have been raised right at the beginning of the recruitment drive regarding a sudden change of the interview venue, causing suffering to many candidates.
Renowned Malaysian manufacturer Top Glove plans to recruit a total of 379 workers from Bangladesh. Verification and interviews for former employees (ex-workers) began on the morning of November 11 at the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Center (BKTTC) in the capital.
Meanwhile, candidate screening and interviews for employer-recommended candidates (referral workers) will be conducted on November 12 directly by the employer.
Combined, both categories aim to fulfill the total recruitment count of 379 workers.
Under the employer's plan, Top Glove will bear all expenses related to visas, medical examinations, and immigration processing for the selected candidates, ensuring zero migration cost for the recruits.
Top Glove actively promoted the recruitment drive across various online platforms.
Advertisements posted on the company’s official LinkedIn and Facebook pages initially stated that interviews for prospective candidates would take place on November 11 and 12 at Madani Avenue in the Bashundhara Residential Area, Dhaka.
Candidates were instructed to bring their passports and necessary documentation.
However, just one day prior to the interviews, a new notice was posted on the company's Facebook page announcing that the venue had been shifted to the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Center (BKTTC).
The abrupt change left many applicants confused. Candidates who had prepared to travel to Madani Avenue in Bashundhara based on the initial announcement had to reorganize their transit plans on short notice.
The situation proved especially problematic for candidates traveling from outside Dhaka, creating anxiety over unexpected travel time and expenses, unfamiliar locations, and the risk of failing to report on schedule.
Several applicants attending the interviews further alleged that their past work experience and skills were not being evaluated properly.
Additionally, candidates noted a lack of clear guidance regarding appeal or review procedures in the event of rejection.
Questions have been raised as to why the venue was changed at the eleventh hour when it had been pre-determined, and whether explicit consent was obtained from the employer prior to making the modification.
BOESL clarifies
When asked about the sudden change during the interviews at BKTTC on Wednesday morning, BOESL managing director Mohammad Rashedul Huq told reporters: "BOESL operates with a specific mandate. As a government agency, we cannot utilize private office spaces to maintain this operational framework, which is why permission was not granted for that venue by the government."
Migration experts, however, contend that simply shifting the interview location does not guarantee transparency in recruitment.
Instead, what matters is whether such changes are logical, transparent, and executed with mutual consensus among all stakeholders.
Decisions taken without prior coordination or consent from the employer could lead to complications in future recruitment pipelines.
Commenting on the matter, migration expert Barrister Humaiun Kabir Pallob emphasized that changes during recruitment processes—whether venue-related or otherwise—must occur through bilateral discussion and mutual agreement.
He warned that a lack of coordination and consensus could deter major foreign employers like Top Glove from pursuing zero-cost recruitment in Bangladesh in the future, ultimately impacting the national overseas employment sector.
He advised BOESL to adopt a more cautious, coordinated, and professional approach when managing such recruitment drives.
Top Glove's focus on ex-workers and referrals
Top Glove’s initiative to select candidates directly—focusing on re-hiring former employees as well as candidates recommended by existing staff—has drawn significant attention.
Stakeholders noted that allowing employers to select candidates based on past experience and internal referrals can increase efficiency.
However, maintaining effective administrative support from BOESL while protecting employer autonomy in candidate selection remains vital.
While the primary objective of zero-cost recruitment is to relieve workers of migration debts, ensuring candidate quality, process transparency, and seamless coordination among all involved parties is equally essential.

item.title: PM visits Bangladesh Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday visited the Bangladesh Pavilion at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where he toured an exhibition of environment-friendly jute products and viewed displays highlighting the country's initiatives to protect the environment.
He visited the pavilion at the conference venue at 4:50pm local time.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo, State Minister Shaikh Faridul Islam and Prime Minister's Special Assistant for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Saimum Parvez welcomed him at the pavilion.
During the visit, Tarique went through displays on various initiatives taken by Bangladesh, including tree plantation, environmental conservation and efforts to address the impacts of climate change.
He also spoke with officials and staff working at the pavilion and enquired about its activities, the products on display and how Bangladesh's climate initiatives are being presented to the international community.
The officials briefed the Prime Minister on the pavilion's activities and various aspects of the exhibition.

item.title: Dooley hails Bangladesh’s performance, calls Farhaan’s goal ‘unbelievable’
item.description:
Bangladesh head coach Thomas Dooley was delighted with his side’s performance after the hosts produced a commanding 4-0 victory over Sri Lanka to finish as Group A winners in the TECNO SAFF Championship 2026 at the National Stadium in Dhaka on Wednesday.
Goals from Shamit Shome, Hamza Choudhury, Farhaan Ali Wahid and Rakib Hossain secured Bangladesh’s second consecutive victory and sent them into Saturday’s semi-finals with maximum points.
Dooley was particularly pleased with the manner in which his team executed their attacking approach, keeping possession, moving the ball quickly and creating one-on-one opportunities in the final third.
“I’m very happy with the results and also with the way we played. That’s what we talked about – how we want to play. We want to play football, let the ball move and be dangerous up front, trying to get into one-on-one situations with Rakib and on the wings also,” Dooley said after the match.
The German-American coach also revealed that he had advised Farhaan at half-time to use his dribbling ability further up the pitch rather than taking unnecessary risks.
The 19-year-old winger, who made his tournament debut against Sri Lanka, responded in spectacular fashion, weaving past several defenders before producing a superb finish seven minutes into the second half.
“What a goal he scored, it’s unbelievable,” Dooley said.
Asked whether Farhaan’s effort was among the best goals he had witnessed during his coaching career, Dooley was unequivocal in his praise.
“Yeah, absolutely. It was really amazing how he dribbled through those three or four guys, and then the shot was also very difficult and it was beautiful,” he said.
The coach also highlighted the quality of the other goals, including Hamza’s second-half involvement in the attacking moves and Rakib’s late strike.
“You can imagine if Hamza’s backheel pass goes in, what kind of goals we had today. Rakib, this is a beautiful goal. So, no, I like overall, from the first until the last minute, we actually can be happy and proud of the players,” he added.
However, the convincing victory came with a concern for Bangladesh, as Dooley revealed that midfielder Saad Uddin had picked up an injury that could rule him out for the remainder of the tournament.
“The bad part is that Saad is injured and maybe he can’t play anymore,” the coach said.
Bangladesh will now face Pakistan in the second semi-final on Saturday, while India and Bhutan meet in the other last-four encounter at the same venue.
